name: ForkUnion
workload: N-body dispatch latency (N=512 bodies, every logical core, 30 s window per cell) and connected-components fork-join frequency (84 dispatches per pass on a ~27M-edge graph).
claimed_speedup: README: ~3-6x faster than OpenMP and ~12-16x faster than Rayon and Taskflow per parallel-for dispatch. On 128x Intel SPR Linux, C++ static/dynamic 54/86 us vs OpenMP 115/226, Rayon 483/739, Taskflow 666/694. On 192x Graviton 5: 47/136 vs OpenMP 266/216. On 24x Intel RPL Windows static, Rayon 151 us vs ForkUnion C++ 148 us (near parity).
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native (CXXFLAGS), Rust target-cpu=native, no LTO, identical kernels
hardware: 18x Apple M5 Pro; 24x Intel RPL (Windows); 128x Intel SPR (Linux); 192x AWS Graviton 5 (Linux); exact CPU SKUs not given
tradeoffs: Not a task-queue runtime: no task graphs, futures, nested parallelism or async I/O; targets tight parallel-for loops. C++17, C99, Rust and Zig bindings.
caveats: Dynamic scheduling column is not always the winner (OpenMP wins on Graviton dynamic 216 vs 136 us; Rayon ties on RPL). Does not benchmark oneTBB although the README table lists it. Windows MinGW-GCC on RPL. Numbers are author's own.
found_via: Hacker News: thread 'Beyond OpenMP in C++ and Rust: Taskflow, Rayon, Fork Union' (item 45402820) via Rayon search; repo README opened

name: citor
baseline: oneTBB (also BS::thread_pool, Taskflow, OpenMP, Eigen::ThreadPool, dispenso, riften)
workload: parallel_bench harness: parallelFor granularity sweeps, forkJoin recursion, scans, reductions, runPlex phases against ten peer pools on one Zen 5 CCD.
claimed_speedup: README says citor wins the vast majority of contested cells on the single-CCD Zen target, remaining differences within single-digit-percent noise; numbers only in SVG charts (geomean heatmaps), no table.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14 / Clang 19 on Ubuntu 24.04 (build flags for the charted run not confirmed)
hardware: single Zen 5 CCD, governor=performance, boost off
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20; Linux x86_64 primary; CPU-bound synchronous engine, no futures; tuned for Zen CCD with pinning.
caveats: README admits losses on larger hosts (multi-CCD AMD, Sapphire Rapids), and on heavy-tailed reductions versus oneTBB. Quantified results only in SVG charts I could not read; no numbers verified on the page. Benchmark code is public (benchmark/parallel_bench) so a verifier can upgrade.
found_via: Hacker News: no thread; surfaced by WebSearch 'C++ work-stealing thread pool benchmark oneTBB' after HN queries

name: Scheduling (dpuyda)
workload: Google Benchmark: recursive Fibonacci n=35, linear chain of 33,554,432 tasks, 2048x2048 matrix multiplication task graph.
claimed_speedup: Fibonacci n=35: 1,661 ms wall vs Taskflow 15,058 ms (derived ~9x). Linear chain: 4,158 ms vs 9,951 ms (derived ~2.4x). Matmul 2048x2048: 4,134 ms vs 3,970 ms (Taskflow slightly faster wall).
hardware: Intel i7-1165G7 (reported as 32 CPUs), Debian GNU/Linux 12
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20, Chase-Lev work-stealing, under 1000 lines, task graphs.
caveats: Compiler and flags not seen on page; paper says performance is 'comparable' to Taskflow. Baseline is Taskflow, not oneTBB. Fibonacci gap looks large and may reflect Taskflow's non-recursive-friendly design. Matmul is not faster. Arxiv blocked here, tier B rests on paper existence, may drop to C.
found_via: Hacker News: query 'Show HN thread pool faster than TBB work stealing C++' web result linked arXiv 2407.15805; repo opened

name: Nexus (huxint)
workload: Single-producer fire-and-forget, sequential submit and retrieve, recursive fork-join, 8-producer submit, round-trip latency, 8 worker threads.
claimed_speedup: Million tasks/s Nexus vs Taskflow vs BS: fire-and-forget 8.39 vs 1.24 vs 0.40; submit+retrieve 2.09 vs 0.38 vs 0.27; recursive fork-join 28.40 vs 8.62 vs 1.23; multi-producer x8 7.60 vs 2.76 vs 1.36; P50/P99 round trip 0.44/0.87 us vs Taskflow 2.66/7.44 us.
tradeoffs: C++26 header-only, work-stealing plus lock-free MPMC, P2300 scheduler compatible; needs very new compiler.
caveats: Table is in README, first-party, flags beyond Release not stated; only 8 threads on a 12650H; Taskflow is not designed for fire-and-forget submit so comparison favors Nexus. Repo is new. Not same as abso1ut3zer0/nexus in known list.
found_via: Hacker News: no thread; WebSearch 'Show HN C++ task scheduler work-stealing benchmark vs oneTBB Taskflow'

name: ThunderBolt-HT
workload: Per-task cost, partitioned parallel_for versus taskflow for_each, and a headless deterministic game-simulation frame graph.
claimed_speedup: Per-task cost 286 ns vs Taskflow 451 ns (1.58x); parallel_for 7-19% faster; Simulation stress scene 0.162 vs 0.195 ms/tick (1.19x).
tradeoffs: C++20, work-stealing deques with dependency-aware scheduling, CMake 3.25+, MSVC/GCC/Clang with pinned toolchain.
caveats: Hardware and flags not found on the page I read; README states a deliberate omission of oneTBB. One repo-local benchmark; very new.

name: dp::thread_pool
workload: 256x256 matrix multiplication task submission across thread pools.
claimed_speedup: MSVC run: dp::thread_pool with std::function 93.27 ms/op vs BS::thread_pool 99.73 ms/op (derived ~7% faster); riften::Thiefpool 93.18 ms/op, README says riften pulls ahead in some cases.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 simple queue pool; not a full work-stealing scheduler by default.
caveats: Tiny margin over BS, essentially tied with riften; no TBB/OpenMP/Rayon baseline. Weak fit for the category baselines; included for coverage.
